SIMEX and MC-SIMEX with mismeasured

Maciej Beresewicz

2026-07-08

Source: vignettes/simex.Rmd
simex.Rmd

Scope

This vignette covers the simulation-extrapolation family of corrections in mismeasured: classical SIMEX for continuous measurement error (Cook & Stefanski, 1994), MC-SIMEX for discrete misclassification (Kuechenhoff, Mwalili & Lesaffre, 2006), and the improved fixed-matrix correction of Sevilimedu & Yu (2026). All are accessed through the single simex() function with a formula interface.

For analytical bias-correction estimators (BCA, BCM, corrected score, one-step) under misclassification, see the companion vignette vignette("mcglm", "mismeasured").

Supported error types

Type Formula syntax Method
Continuous measurement error me(x, sd) SIMEX (Cook & Stefanski, 1994)
Berkson measurement error me(x, sd, type = "berkson") Berkson SIMEX
Systematic (non-zero mean) ME me(x, sd, mean = mu) Non-zero mean SIMEX
Discrete misclassification mc(z, Pi) MC-SIMEX (Kuechenhoff et al., 2006)
Improved misclassification mc(z, Pi), method = "improved" Sevilimedu & Yu (2026)
Response misclassification mc(y, Pi_y) ~ ... MC-SIMEX on response

Supported families

gaussian(), poisson(), binomial() (canonical links).

Background: the SIMEX algorithm

When a covariate XX is measured with additive error W=X+UW = X + U, U∼N(0,σu2)U \sim N(0, \sigma_u^2), regression coefficients are biased toward zero (attenuation bias). SIMEX corrects this in two steps:

  1. Simulation. For λ∈{0.5,1,1.5,2}\lambda \in \{0.5, 1, 1.5, 2\} and b=1,…,Bb = 1, \ldots, B, generate Wb,λ*=W+λ⋅UbW^*_{b,\lambda} = W + \sqrt{\lambda} \cdot U_b with Ub∼N(0,σu2)U_b \sim N(0, \sigma_u^2). Refit the model on each pseudo-dataset.

  2. Extrapolation. Fit a polynomial (quadratic, linear, or loglinear) to β̂‾(λ)\bar{\hat\beta}(\lambda) as a function of λ\lambda and extrapolate to λ=−1\lambda = -1, the value implying no measurement error.

For misclassification, the MC-SIMEX algorithm replaces additive noise with resampling from Πλ\Pi^\lambda, the misclassification matrix raised to fractional powers. The improved method computes a closed-form correction factor c(λ)c(\lambda) in place of the parametric extrapolation.

Example 1: Continuous measurement error 

n <- 2000
x_true <- rnorm(n)
y <- 1 + 2 * x_true + rnorm(n, sd = 0.5)
x_obs <- x_true + rnorm(n, sd = 0.5)
df <- data.frame(y = y, x = x_obs)

naive <- lm(y ~ x, data = df)
fit   <- simex(y ~ me(x, 0.5), data = df, B = 200, seed = 42)

cat("True slope:  2.000\n")
#> True slope:  2.000
cat("Naive slope:", round(coef(naive)["x"], 3), "\n")
#> Naive slope: 1.578
cat("SIMEX slope:", round(coef(fit)["x"], 3), "\n")
#> SIMEX slope: 1.915

Summary, inference, and trajectory 

summary(fit)
#> 
#> Call:
#> simex(formula = y ~ me(x, 0.5), data = df, B = 200, seed = 42)
#> 
#> Family: gaussian 
#> SIMEX variable(s): x 
#> Extrapolation: quadratic 
#> Lambda grid: 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2 
#> B = 200 , n = 2000 
#> 
#> Residuals:
#>      Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
#> -3.38970 -0.78080 -0.02356  0.79428  3.25930 
#> 
#> Naive coefficients:
#> (Intercept)           x 
#>      0.9843      1.5779 
#> 
#> SIMEX corrected coefficients:
#>             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
#> (Intercept)  0.98948    0.02418   40.92   <2e-16 ***
#> x            1.91518    0.02453   78.08   <2e-16 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
confint(fit)
#>                 2.5 %   97.5 %
#> (Intercept) 0.9420865 1.036866
#> x           1.8671012 1.963252
plot(fit)

The plot shows coefficient estimates at each λ\lambda level (solid points), the naive estimate at λ=0\lambda = 0 (open circle), the extrapolation curve, and the corrected estimate at λ=−1\lambda = -1 (red cross).

Refitting with a different extrapolation 

fit_lin <- refit(fit, extrapolation = "linear")
cat("Quadratic:", round(coef(fit)["x"], 3), "\n")
#> Quadratic: 1.915
cat("Linear:   ", round(coef(fit_lin)["x"], 3), "\n")
#> Linear:    1.78

Example 2: Multiple error-prone covariates 

x1_true <- rnorm(n); x2_true <- rnorm(n)
y <- 1 + 1.5 * x1_true - 0.8 * x2_true + rnorm(n, sd = 0.5)
df2 <- data.frame(
  y  = y,
  x1 = x1_true + rnorm(n, sd = 0.3),
  x2 = x2_true + rnorm(n, sd = 0.5)
)
fit2 <- simex(y ~ me(x1, 0.3) + me(x2, 0.5), data = df2, B = 200, seed = 42)
summary(fit2)
#> 
#> Call:
#> simex(formula = y ~ me(x1, 0.3) + me(x2, 0.5), data = df2, B = 200, 
#>     seed = 42)

#> B = 200 , n = 2000 
#> 
#> Residuals:
#>       Min        1Q    Median        3Q       Max 
#> -2.431169 -0.525458  0.008814  0.508883  2.844247 
#> 
#> Naive coefficients:
#> (Intercept)          x1          x2 
#>      0.9901      1.3756     -0.6430 
#> 
#> SIMEX corrected coefficients:
#>             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
#> (Intercept)  0.99644    0.01751   56.92   <2e-16 ***
#> x1           1.48999    0.01691   88.13   <2e-16 ***
#> x2          -0.77492    0.01739  -44.55   <2e-16 ***
#> ---

Example 3: Misclassification (standard MC-SIMEX)

A binary covariate ZZ is misclassified with known matrix Π\Pi, Πjℓ=Pr⁡(Z*=j∣Z=ℓ)\Pi_{j\ell} = \Pr(Z^* = j \mid Z = \ell).

z <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.4)
y3 <- 1 + 2 * z + 0.5 * rnorm(n) + rnorm(n)

z_star <- z
z_star[z == 0] <- rbinom(sum(z == 0), 1, 0.10)
z_star[z == 1] <- 1 - rbinom(sum(z == 1), 1, 0.15)

Pi <- matrix(c(0.9, 0.1, 0.15, 0.85), 2, 2)
df3 <- data.frame(y = y3, z = factor(z_star))

fit3 <- simex(y ~ mc(z, Pi), data = df3, method = "standard",
              B = 200, seed = 42)

cat("True z effect:     2.000\n")
#> True z effect:     2.000
cat("Naive z effect:   ", round(fit3$naive.coefficients[1], 3), "\n")
#> Naive z effect:    1.485
cat("MC-SIMEX z effect:", round(coef(fit3)[1], 3), "\n")
#> MC-SIMEX z effect: 1.962

Example 4: Improved MC-SIMEX (exact correction)

The improved method (Sevilimedu & Yu, 2026) computes an exact fixed-matrix correction instead of extrapolation. It needs only B=1B = 1 replicate and is the default for a single misclassified covariate. For binary covariates the correction factor is reported as c.lambda; for KK-level factors the dummy-coefficient correction matrix is stored in correction.matrix.

fit4 <- simex(y ~ mc(z, Pi), data = df3, seed = 42)  # default: improved

cat("Method:", fit4$method, "\n")
#> Method: improved
cat("Correction factor c(lambda):", round(fit4$c.lambda, 4), "\n")
#> Correction factor c(lambda): 1.7954
cat("Improved z effect:", round(coef(fit4)[1], 3), "\n")
#> Improved z effect: 2.001

Optimal lambda

The improved method can search for the lambda that minimizes the absolute correction factor:

fit4_opt <- simex(y ~ mc(z, Pi), data = df3, lambda = "optimal", seed = 42)
cat("Optimal lambda:", fit4_opt$lambda[-1], "\n")
#> Optimal lambda: 0.1
cat("Optimal c(lambda):", round(fit4_opt$c.lambda, 4), "\n")
#> Optimal c(lambda): 1.3808

Example 5: Multiple misclassified covariates 

z1 <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.4); z2 <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.6)
y5 <- 1 + 2 * z1 + 1.5 * z2 + rnorm(n)

z1_star <- z1
z1_star[z1 == 0] <- rbinom(sum(z1 == 0), 1, 0.10)
z1_star[z1 == 1] <- 1 - rbinom(sum(z1 == 1), 1, 0.15)
z2_star <- z2
z2_star[z2 == 0] <- rbinom(sum(z2 == 0), 1, 0.08)
z2_star[z2 == 1] <- 1 - rbinom(sum(z2 == 1), 1, 0.12)

Pi1 <- matrix(c(0.9, 0.1, 0.15, 0.85), 2, 2)
Pi2 <- matrix(c(0.92, 0.08, 0.12, 0.88), 2, 2)
df5 <- data.frame(y = y5, z1 = factor(z1_star), z2 = factor(z2_star))

fit5 <- simex(y ~ mc(z1, Pi1) + mc(z2, Pi2), data = df5,
              method = "standard", B = 200, seed = 42)
summary(fit5)
#> 
#> Call:
#> simex(formula = y ~ mc(z1, Pi1) + mc(z2, Pi2), data = df5, method = "standard", 
#>     B = 200, seed = 42)
#> 
#> Family: gaussian 
#> MC-SIMEX variables: z1, z2 
#> Method: standard 
#> Extrapolation: quadratic 
#> Lambda grid: 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2 
#> B = 200 , n = 2000 
#> 
#> Residuals:
#>      Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
#> -5.04944 -0.79086  0.06307  0.86372  5.21285 
#> 
#> Naive coefficients:
#>         z11         z21 (Intercept) 
#>      1.5543      1.2123      1.3934 
#> 
#> MC-SIMEX corrected coefficients:
#>             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
#> z11          2.05372    0.08077   25.43   <2e-16 ***
#> z21          1.53946    0.07239   21.27   <2e-16 ***
#> (Intercept)  0.95523    0.06339   15.07   <2e-16 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

With multiple mc() terms, the standard method is used automatically; each variable is resampled independently via its own misclassification matrix.

Example 6: Response misclassification

When the outcome itself is misclassified, use mc() on the left-hand side:

x6 <- rnorm(n)
y6_true <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-0.5 + 1.2 * x6))
y6_obs <- y6_true
y6_obs[y6_true == 0] <- rbinom(sum(y6_true == 0), 1, 0.10)
y6_obs[y6_true == 1] <- 1 - rbinom(sum(y6_true == 1), 1, 0.08)

Pi_y <- matrix(c(0.90, 0.10, 0.08, 0.92), 2, 2)
df6 <- data.frame(y = factor(y6_obs), x = x6)

fit6 <- simex(mc(y, Pi_y) ~ x, family = binomial(), data = df6,
              B = 200, seed = 42)

cat("True x effect:     1.200\n")
#> True x effect:     1.200
cat("Naive x effect:   ", round(fit6$naive.coefficients["x"], 3), "\n")
#> Naive x effect:    0.9
cat("MC-SIMEX x effect:", round(coef(fit6)["x"], 3), "\n")
#> MC-SIMEX x effect: 1.175

Response misclassification can be combined with covariate misclassification:

z6 <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.4)
y6b_true <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-0.5 + 1.0 * z6 + 0.5 * x6))
y6b_obs <- y6b_true
y6b_obs[y6b_true == 0] <- rbinom(sum(y6b_true == 0), 1, 0.10)
y6b_obs[y6b_true == 1] <- 1 - rbinom(sum(y6b_true == 1), 1, 0.08)

z6_star <- z6
z6_star[z6 == 0] <- rbinom(sum(z6 == 0), 1, 0.10)
z6_star[z6 == 1] <- 1 - rbinom(sum(z6 == 1), 1, 0.15)

df6b <- data.frame(y = factor(y6b_obs), z = factor(z6_star), x = x6)
fit6b <- simex(mc(y, Pi_y) ~ mc(z, Pi) + x, family = binomial(),
               data = df6b, B = 200, seed = 42)
summary(fit6b)
#> 
#> Call:
#> simex(formula = mc(y, Pi_y) ~ mc(z, Pi) + x, family = binomial(), 
#>     data = df6b, B = 200, seed = 42)
#> 
#> Family: binomial 
#> MC-SIMEX variable: z 
#> Method: standard 
#> Extrapolation: quadratic 
#> Lambda grid: 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2 
#> B = 200 , n = 2000 
#> 
#> Residuals:
#>     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
#> -0.8432 -0.4503 -0.2201  0.4895  0.8450 
#> 
#> Naive coefficients:
#>          z1 (Intercept)           x 
#>      0.4873     -0.2085      0.3293 
#> 
#> MC-SIMEX corrected coefficients:
#>             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
#> z1           0.75905    0.13445   5.646 1.88e-08 ***
#> (Intercept) -0.35817    0.07936  -4.513 6.76e-06 ***
#> x            0.39681    0.05843   6.791 1.46e-11 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Example 7: Berkson measurement error

In the Berkson model the true value is a noisy version of the observed (assigned) value: X=W+UX = W + U.

w <- rnorm(n)
u <- rnorm(n, sd = 0.5)
x_true_b <- w + u
y7 <- 1 + 2 * x_true_b + rnorm(n, sd = 0.5)
df7 <- data.frame(y = y7, x = w)

fit7_class <- simex(y ~ me(x, 0.5), data = df7, B = 200, seed = 42)
fit7_berk  <- simex(y ~ me(x, 0.5, type = "berkson"), data = df7,
                    B = 200, seed = 42)

cat("Classical SIMEX slope:", round(coef(fit7_class)["x"], 3), "\n")
#> Classical SIMEX slope: 2.567
cat("Berkson SIMEX slope:  ", round(coef(fit7_berk)["x"], 3), "\n")
#> Berkson SIMEX slope:   2.562

Example 8: Non-zero mean measurement error

When measurement error has a systematic component U∼N(μ,σ2)U \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2) with μ≠0\mu \neq 0:

x_true_m <- rnorm(n)
x_obs_m <- x_true_m + rnorm(n, mean = 0.3, sd = 0.5)
y8 <- 1 + 2 * x_true_m + rnorm(n, sd = 0.5)
df8 <- data.frame(y = y8, x = x_obs_m)

fit8_std <- simex(y ~ me(x, 0.5), data = df8, B = 200, seed = 42)
fit8_nzm <- simex(y ~ me(x, 0.5, mean = 0.3), data = df8, B = 200, seed = 42)

cat("Standard SIMEX (ignoring mean):", round(coef(fit8_std)["x"], 3), "\n")
#> Standard SIMEX (ignoring mean): 1.938
cat("Non-zero mean SIMEX:           ", round(coef(fit8_nzm)["x"], 3), "\n")
#> Non-zero mean SIMEX:            1.938

Example 9: Poisson regression with misclassification 

z9 <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.4)
y9 <- rpois(n, exp(0.5 + 0.8 * z9))

z9_star <- z9
z9_star[z9 == 0] <- rbinom(sum(z9 == 0), 1, 0.10)
z9_star[z9 == 1] <- 1 - rbinom(sum(z9 == 1), 1, 0.15)

df9 <- data.frame(y = y9, z = factor(z9_star))
fit9 <- simex(y ~ mc(z, Pi), family = poisson(), data = df9, seed = 42)
summary(fit9)
#>

Example 10: Frequency weights

The weights argument supports frequency (prior) weights:

df10_agg <- data.frame(
  y = c(2.5, 3.1, 4.2, 5.0),
  x = c(1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0),
  freq = c(100, 150, 120, 130)
)
fit10 <- simex(y ~ me(x, 0.3), data = df10_agg, weights = df10_agg$freq,
               B = 100, seed = 42)
coef(fit10)
#> (Intercept)           x 
#>   1.4042179   0.9413936

Utility functions

Building misclassification matrices

build.mc.matrix() finds the nearest valid misclassification matrix (one that can be raised to fractional powers without negative probabilities):

Pi_empirical <- matrix(c(0.85, 0.10, 0.05,
                          0.10, 0.80, 0.10,
                          0.05, 0.10, 0.85), 3, 3, byrow = TRUE)
check.mc.matrix(list(Pi_empirical))
#> [1] TRUE

Pi_valid <- build.mc.matrix(Pi_empirical)
check.mc.matrix(list(Pi_valid))
#> [1] TRUE

Checking matrix validity 

P1 <- matrix(c(0.9, 0.1, 0.2, 0.8), 2, 2)
P2 <- matrix(c(0.4, 0.6, 0.6, 0.4), 2, 2)  # too much error
check.mc.matrix(list(P1, P2))
#> [1]  TRUE FALSE

Implementation details

C++ backend

The simulation step runs in C++ via Rcpp/RcppEigen for all error types:

  • simex_sim_cpp — continuous ME with IRLS fitting plus model-vcov accumulation
  • mcsimex_sim_cpp — single-variable MC-SIMEX
  • mcsimex_multi_sim_cpp — multi-variable MC-SIMEX with optional response mc

The IRLS solver supports Gaussian, Poisson, and Binomial canonical links. Matrix exponentiation for Πλ\Pi^\lambda uses eigendecomposition.

Variance estimation

  • ME-SIMEX. Jackknife variance following Stefanski & Cook (1994). The model-based variance V‾model(λ)\bar V_{\mathrm{model}}(\lambda) is the average of (Xsim′WXsim)−1ϕ(X_{\mathrm{sim}}'WX_{\mathrm{sim}})^{-1}\phi across BB refits, computed in C++. Vjk(λ)=V‾model−Cov̂(θ̂b)V_{\mathrm{jk}}(\lambda) = \bar V_{\mathrm{model}} - \widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}(\hat\theta_b) is then extrapolated to λ=−1\lambda = -1.
  • MC-SIMEX standard. The same jackknife approach with sandwich variance at the mean estimate per lambda.
  • MC-SIMEX improved. Scaled model-based variance: Vcorrected=c(λ)2VmodelV_{\mathrm{corrected}} = c(\lambda)^2 V_{\mathrm{model}}.

When to use what

  • Continuous additive error, known σu\sigma_u. me(x, sd). Quadratic extrapolation is the default; use extrapolation = "linear" for stability when the curvature is poorly estimated.
  • Berkson assignment error. me(x, sd, type = "berkson").
  • Systematic bias on top of additive noise. me(x, sd, mean = mu).
  • Single misclassified factor. mc(z, Pi). Default is the improved fixed-matrix correction; use method = "standard" for the original Kuechenhoff et al. extrapolation if your downstream tooling expects it.
  • Multiple misclassified factors or misclassified response. simex() automatically falls back to the standard MC-SIMEX path.

References

Cook, J. R. and Stefanski, L. A. (1994). Simulation-extrapolation estimation in parametric measurement error models. J. Amer. Statist. Assoc. 89(428), 1314–1328.

Kuechenhoff, H., Mwalili, S. M. and Lesaffre, E. (2006). A general method for dealing with misclassification in regression: the misclassification SIMEX. Biometrics 62(1), 85–96.

Sevilimedu, V. and Yu, L. (2026). An improved misclassification simulation extrapolation (MC-SIMEX) algorithm. Statistics in Medicine 45, e70418.

Stefanski, L. A. and Cook, J. R. (1995). Simulation-extrapolation: the measurement error jackknife. J. Amer. Statist. Assoc. 90(432), 1247–1256.
